BEARERS OF A MESSAGE TO THE KING.

Four Basuto chiefs arrived in London on Saturday with a counsellor, two interpreters and an assistant interpreter of the same nation. They bring a loyal message from Letsia, the paramount chief of the Basutos, to the King, and will lay before the Colonial Office the views of the national council on the position that Basutoland should occupy in the new federated South Africa.

The Colonial Office is determined that the chiefs shall carry back a good impression of the hospitality of the British nation. Three smart carriages met the visitors at Waterloo and conveyed them to a handsomely furnished house in Bayswater, close to Hyde Park. Here they will be well looked after by a firm of wholesale providers, who will see to their entertainment out of doors as well as their comfort at home. The chiefs had not been installed in these comfortable quarters many hours before a fashionable tailor arrived, sent by the Colonial Office, to take their orders.

Seeiso, the leader of the deputation, is a son of Letsia Moshesh, a former paramount chief, and uncle to the present head of the Basutos. He is a man of great girth and height, caretaker of the Mafeteng District, and owner of great wealth in cattle, sheep, goats, and horses. His age is fifty-six.

The remaining members of the deputa-tion are Seciso's brother Mojela, sixty-one years old; his nephew Masupha, twenty-seven; and his cousin Leshoboro, fifty-two. "It is the first time they have been out of their country," said the Government interpreter on Saturday, "and they do not understand why anyone should be interested in what they do here. They say it is very cold. It is settled that they will see the King, but the day has not yet been decided. They do not know how long they will stay in England. Perhaps two or three weeks."
